first.paragraphOne: This month’s improvements focus on the small moments that make managing your online work feel clearer. Dashboard navigation is more consistent, recent activity is easier to review, and important service information stays close to the work it describes.
first.paragraphTwo: We also refined how complementary services appear across Unixsee. SEO, graphic design, product data entry, and social media support now use a shared structure, making it easier to understand where work is happening and what changed.

second.title: What comes next
second.paragraphOne: The next round of improvements will continue to connect notifications with the pages they describe. Each story will provide enough context to understand the update without turning the experience into an urgent alert or operational task.
second.paragraphTwo: Your feedback continues to shape these refinements. As the dashboard evolves, we will keep prioritizing calm communication, predictable navigation, and information that is useful when you choose to read it.

first.title: Build strong search foundations
first.paragraphOne: Search visibility starts with pages that answer a clear question well. Give every important page one focused purpose, a descriptive title, and a summary that helps people understand what they will find before they open it.
first.paragraphTwo: Technical health matters too. Stable page addresses, descriptive links, useful alternative text, and fast loading give search engines a clearer view of the site while also improving the experience for visitors.

second.title: Create a repeatable review routine
second.paragraphOne: Review performance on a regular schedule instead of reacting to isolated changes. Look for pages that steadily gain impressions, queries that bring the right audience, and content that receives attention but does not yet lead to meaningful engagement.
second.paragraphTwo: Use those signals to update the most valuable pages first. Small improvements to clarity, internal links, and content depth are easier to measure and maintain than a large collection of disconnected SEO changes.

first.title: Clarity before decoration
first.paragraphOne: The strongest work in this month’s selection uses hierarchy before ornament. Confident headings, deliberate spacing, and a restrained color palette help the message arrive quickly without making the composition feel plain.
first.paragraphTwo: Editorial layouts are also becoming more flexible. Large type, compact supporting details, and modular image areas create personality while still adapting cleanly to smaller screens and translated content.

second.title: Designing as a system
second.paragraphOne: A memorable visual direction becomes more useful when it can repeat. Reusable spacing, typography, image treatments, and component patterns make each new asset feel connected without forcing every piece to look identical.
second.paragraphTwo: When reviewing new work, test the system with both short and long content. A design that remains balanced in English and Persian is more resilient and easier to extend across future campaigns.

first.title: Formats people finish
first.paragraphOne: Audiences are responding to content that reaches its point quickly and rewards continued attention. Short demonstrations, focused carousels, and concise explanations work best when every frame contributes to one clear idea.
first.paragraphTwo: The opening still matters, but a strong hook should accurately represent the rest of the story. Clear expectations build more durable attention than exaggerated promises that the content cannot support.

second.title: Consistency over volume
second.paragraphOne: A recognizable publishing rhythm is often more valuable than posting as frequently as possible. Consistent topics, visual cues, and tone help the right audience understand what they can expect from the brand.
second.paragraphTwo: Choose a small group of repeatable formats, review how people respond, and refine them over time. This creates a practical content system while leaving room for timely ideas and experimentation.

whatIsTtfb.lede: TTFB — Time to First Byte — measures how long a browser waits before it receives the first byte of a server response. It is one of the earliest signals of site performance.
whatIsTtfb.p1: When a browser makes a request to your site, the server must receive it, process it, and begin sending a response. TTFB counts only the time until that first byte arrives — not how long the full page takes to load.
whatIsTtfb.p2: Several delays accumulate before any content is sent:
whatIsTtfb.l1: DNS lookup — translating the domain name to a server IP address.
whatIsTtfb.l2: TCP and TLS handshakes — establishing and securing the connection.
whatIsTtfb.l3: Time to send the request — usually very short on modern connections.
whatIsTtfb.l4: Server processing time — generating or retrieving the response.
whatIsTtfb.h3: When is TTFB a sign of a problem?
whatIsTtfb.p3: For a cached static response, a TTFB above 200 ms is worth investigating. For uncached dynamic pages, values up to 500 ms are common and expected.
whatIsTtfb.n1: TTFB alone does not describe the full user experience. Rendering, JavaScript execution, and image loading all affect what users see, but none of these are reflected in TTFB.
whatIsTtfb.p4: TTFB is sensitive to network conditions between the user and the server. A user on a mobile connection far from the data center will always see a higher TTFB than a fiber user next to it. Use a CDN to bring content closer to your audience.
whatIsTtfb.k1: TTFB measures the time until the first byte of a server response arrives.
whatIsTtfb.k2: A high TTFB on a cached page is a useful signal; a high TTFB on an uncached dynamic page is expected.
whatIsTtfb.k3: Network distance, DNS, TLS, and server processing all add to TTFB.

firstChecks.purpose: Run through these checks before spending time on deeper performance analysis. Each one is quick to confirm and covers the most common causes of a suddenly slow site.
firstChecks.c1: Reproduce the issue in an incognito window without extensions to rule out a local cache or plugin conflict.
firstChecks.c2: Check the monitoring timeline for any downtime or elevated response times in the last 24 hours.
firstChecks.c3: Test with a tool such as GTmetrix or PageSpeed Insights to get an objective baseline measurement.
firstChecks.c4: Verify that page caching is active and returning cached responses for anonymous visitors.
firstChecks.c5: Check for a recent change: plugin update, theme change, content import, or traffic spike.
firstChecks.tip: Run speed checks from a data center in the same region as your customers for a more representative result.
firstChecks.after: If all five checks pass and the site is still slow, open the performance topic for deeper investigation guides.

whenPurge.scope: Cache purging clears stored responses and forces your server to rebuild them fresh. Knowing when to purge prevents unnecessary load and avoids clearing caches that are still serving users correctly.
whenPurge.r1a: You published or updated a page and the old version is still visible
whenPurge.r1b: Purge the cache for that URL only
whenPurge.r2a: A plugin or theme update changed global layout or CSS
whenPurge.r3a: Prices, inventory, or time-sensitive data are stale
whenPurge.r3b: Purge specific URLs or object-cache keys
whenPurge.h2: Running a full purge via WP-CLI
whenPurge.p2: Use WP-CLI when you need to purge from the command line or from a script:
whenPurge.cap: Clears all cached objects and page cache entries.
whenPurge.n1: A full purge causes a brief spike in server load while pages are rebuilt. For high-traffic stores, purge individual URLs where possible, or schedule a full purge outside peak hours.
whenPurge.k1: Purge individual URLs first; full-site purges cause a short load spike.
whenPurge.k2: Purge immediately after publishing changes that must be visible to all users.

whatIsCache.lede: Understand how caching works and why it is important for improving WooCommerce store performance.
whatIsCache.p1: Caching is a technique that stores frequently requested data so it can be delivered faster without repeating the same processing every time a visitor requests a page.
whatIsCache.p2: For WooCommerce stores, caching helps reduce unnecessary server work and improves the speed of common customer interactions.
whatIsCache.p3: When a visitor opens a page, the system can either generate the response from the application or serve a previously stored version from cache.
whatIsCache.p4: Page caching stores generated page responses so future visitors can receive the content faster without requiring WordPress and WooCommerce to rebuild the page every time.
whatIsCache.p5: Object caching stores frequently used data from the application, such as database query results, so repeated operations can complete faster.
whatIsCache.l2: Improves page loading speed for visitors.
whatIsCache.l3: Helps stores handle more traffic efficiently.
whatIsCache.p6: Cache may need to be cleared after important changes such as updating website design, changing configuration, or modifying content that should appear immediately.
whatIsCache.k1: Caching stores reusable data to improve performance.
whatIsCache.k2: Different cache layers improve different parts of the WooCommerce experience.
whatIsCache.k3: Correct cache management helps maintain a fast and reliable store.

whatIsUnixsee.p1: Unixsee is a managed WooCommerce infrastructure platform designed to help store owners run their online stores with less technical complexity.
whatIsUnixsee.p2: It combines managed infrastructure, monitoring, and operational tools to provide better visibility into website health and performance.
whatIsUnixsee.p3: Unixsee connects your WooCommerce environment with tools that help you understand the current state of your store.
whatIsUnixsee.p4: Unixsee provides an environment prepared for WooCommerce workloads such as products, orders, customer activity, and traffic changes.
whatIsUnixsee.p5: Unixsee monitors important signals such as availability, response time, SSL status, and operational events.
whatIsUnixsee.k1: Unixsee is built for WooCommerce infrastructure.
whatIsUnixsee.k2: It provides visibility into website health and performance.
whatIsUnixsee.k3: It helps store owners manage operations more effectively.

stack.lede: Understand the technology layers that power a managed WooCommerce store on Unixsee.
stack.p1: The managed stack is the combination of server technologies, application services, and configurations that work together to run your WooCommerce store.
stack.p2: Instead of manually configuring each layer, Unixsee manages the underlying environment so your store can run on infrastructure prepared for ecommerce workloads.
stack.p3: A WooCommerce store depends on multiple layers working together. Each layer has a specific responsibility in delivering a reliable shopping experience.
stack.p4: The web server receives customer requests and delivers website content. Unixsee configures this layer to handle common WooCommerce traffic patterns efficiently.
stack.p5: WooCommerce and WordPress run on PHP. The PHP environment controls how your store processes requests, executes plugins, and generates dynamic content.
stack.p6: The database stores important WooCommerce information such as products, orders, customers, settings, and website configuration data.
stack.h6: Why does the managed stack matter?
stack.p7: A managed stack reduces the complexity of maintaining the technical environment behind your store and provides a more consistent foundation for daily operations.
stack.l1: A WooCommerce-focused environment instead of a generic server setup.
stack.l2: Managed configuration across important infrastructure layers.
stack.l3: Better visibility into the systems supporting your store.
stack.k1: The managed stack combines multiple technologies required to run WooCommerce.
stack.k2: Each infrastructure layer has a specific role in store operation.
stack.k3: Unixsee manages the underlying environment so teams can focus on their business.

phpVersions.lede: Learn how Unixsee manages PHP versions and how to choose a compatible version for your WooCommerce store.
phpVersions.p1: PHP is the programming language that powers WordPress and WooCommerce. The PHP version running on your server affects compatibility, security, and application performance.
phpVersions.p2: Unixsee provides supported PHP environments designed to run WooCommerce stores reliably while keeping the underlying platform maintained.
phpVersions.p3: Supported PHP versions depend on your service environment and the compatibility requirements of your WordPress and WooCommerce setup.
phpVersions.l1: Current PHP versions recommended for modern WordPress and WooCommerce installations.
phpVersions.l2: Stable PHP versions maintained for compatibility and security.
phpVersions.l3: Version choices that allow teams to test compatibility before changes are applied.
phpVersions.p4: Changing PHP versions can affect WordPress core, themes, and plugins. Always review compatibility before switching the runtime environment.
phpVersions.l4: Check that your WordPress version supports the target PHP version.
phpVersions.l5: Confirm that important plugins and themes are compatible.
phpVersions.l6: Test changes in a staging environment when possible.
phpVersions.k1: PHP versions affect WordPress and WooCommerce compatibility.
phpVersions.k2: Choose versions based on security, support, and application requirements.
phpVersions.k3: Test PHP changes before applying them to a production store.

checks.lede: Understand how Unixsee checks website availability and detects problems before they affect your store operations.
checks.p1: Uptime checks regularly test whether your website is reachable and responding correctly. They provide visibility into availability and help identify interruptions quickly.
checks.p2: Unixsee uses monitoring checks to verify important website signals and record availability events over time.
checks.p3: An uptime check sends a request to your website at regular intervals and evaluates the response to determine whether the service is available.
checks.p4: The monitoring system sends a request to the configured website address and checks whether the server responds successfully.
checks.p5: The response is evaluated based on availability signals such as successful responses, response time, and detected errors.
checks.p6: If a check fails, Unixsee records the event and provides information that helps you understand when the issue started and how it changed.
checks.l1: Identify when a website becomes unavailable.
checks.l2: Track availability history and incident periods.
checks.l3: Review performance signals during website issues.
checks.k1: Uptime checks verify that your website is reachable and responding.
checks.k2: Monitoring history helps identify availability problems.
checks.k3: Regular checks provide visibility into website reliability.

firewall.lede: Learn how the Unixsee firewall helps protect WooCommerce stores by monitoring requests and blocking suspicious activity.
firewall.p1: A firewall is a security layer that examines incoming requests before they reach your website application. It helps identify and block potentially harmful traffic.
firewall.p2: For WooCommerce stores, a firewall helps reduce exposure to common attacks while allowing normal customer activity such as browsing products and placing orders.
firewall.p3: The firewall analyzes incoming traffic and applies security rules to decide whether a request should be allowed, challenged, or blocked.
firewall.p4: Each request is evaluated using available security signals such as request patterns, source information, and known threat indicators.
firewall.p5: When traffic matches known attack patterns or violates security rules, the firewall can prevent the request from reaching your website.
firewall.p6: Firewall rules are designed to protect important parts of your website while minimizing impact on legitimate visitors and store operations.
firewall.l1: Detect suspicious requests before they reach your application.
firewall.l2: Reduce exposure to common web attacks.
firewall.l3: Protect website availability and customer experience.
firewall.k1: The firewall filters incoming requests using security rules.
firewall.k2: Suspicious traffic can be blocked before reaching WooCommerce.
firewall.k3: Firewall protection helps maintain a safer store environment.

migrateSite.lede: Learn how to move your WooCommerce store to Unixsee infrastructure and prepare for a smooth migration.
migrateSite.p1: Migrating a website means moving your WordPress files, database, and configuration from your current hosting environment to Unixsee.
migrateSite.p2: A successful migration keeps important store data available, including products, orders, customers, settings, and website content.
migrateSite.p3: Before starting the migration process, review your current website configuration and prepare the information required for a successful transfer.
migrateSite.l1: Confirm your domain and DNS settings.
migrateSite.l2: Review WordPress, WooCommerce, and plugin compatibility.
migrateSite.l3: Create a backup of your current website before making changes.
migrateSite.p4: The migration process includes transferring website files, importing the database, configuring the new environment, and verifying that the store works correctly.
migrateSite.p5: Website files and database information are transferred to the Unixsee environment while maintaining important WooCommerce data and configuration settings.
migrateSite.p6: After the migration is complete, important store functions should be tested before directing all visitors to the new environment.
migrateSite.p7: After confirming that the migrated store works correctly, DNS settings can be updated to point your domain to Unixsee infrastructure.
migrateSite.k1: Migration moves your website files, database, and configuration to Unixsee.
migrateSite.k2: Testing is important before switching customer traffic.
migrateSite.k3: A careful migration helps maintain store availability and data integrity.
